withheld.headline: Syria declares ceasefire in parts of Aleppo after days of clashes
withheld.evidence: The Syrian government announced a ceasefire in several neighborhoods of Aleppo early Friday after days of deadly clashes between Syrian forces and Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). In a statement, the Syrian Defense Ministry said the ceasefire was introduced “to prevent any slide towards a new military escalation within residential neighborhoods.” The truce took effect at 3:00 a.m. local time and covers the Sheikh Maqsoud, Ashrafieh, and Bani Zeid districts of northern Aleppo. The ministry emphasized that the decision is part of broader efforts to de-escalate tensions and stabilize the situation in the city. According to the announcement, internal security forces, working alongside the Syrian army, will oversee mechanisms for the withdrawal of armed groups from the affected neighborhoods toward northeastern Syria. Authorities said the move aims to restore calm, reestablish state authority, and prepare conditions for the return of civilian life and rule of law in the impacted areas, following several days of violence that heightened fears of renewed urban conflict in Aleppo. The clashes had raised regional concern due to Aleppo’s history as one of the most contested battlegrounds of Syria’s long-running conflict. withheld.headline: Bangladesh flood death toll rises to 44 as more than one million people affected
withheld.evidence: Relentless monsoon rains, flash floods and landslides have left at least 44 people dead and affected more than one million people across seven districts in Bangladesh, authorities said on Sunday, as emergency responders continued relief operations amid warnings of further flooding. According to the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief, more than 1.022 million people have been affected by the flooding, with 267,918 families remaining stranded by rising waters. At least 39 people have been injured since the severe weather began. The worst-hit districts include Khagrachhari, Rangamati, Bandarban, Cox's Bazar, Chattogram, Moulvibazar and Habiganj, where floodwaters have inundated 58 sub-districts (upazilas), damaging homes, roads, bridges and other critical infrastructure. Although rainfall eased over the past 24 hours in several parts of the country, flood risks remain elevated. The Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre (FFWC) warned that fresh short-term flooding could occur in Feni, Sylhet and northern districts, particularly along the Teesta River basin, due to continued upstream inflows and additional rainfall. The agency said water levels at seven monitoring stations on the Sangu, Matamuhuri, Kushiyara, Manu and Someswari rivers remained above danger levels, keeping low-lying communities at risk. Authorities have opened 1,131 emergency shelters, where 44,457 displaced people are currently staying after being evacuated from flood-affected areas. The Disaster Management Ministry said it had allocated 145 million taka ($1.2 million) and 2,650 metric tonnes of rice to the seven worst-hit districts to support relief efforts. Since July 7, district administrations across the country have also received 345 million taka and 6,900 metric tonnes of rice for emergency response operations. withheld.headline: Alberta Court of Appeal says Ottawa's Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional | CBC News
withheld.evidence: The Alberta Court of Appeal has ruled the federal government's Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional. This was the second time the province of Alberta had challenged the act, which sets out a process to review the environmental, economic, health and social effects of proposed projects like ports, mines and pipelines. In a 4-1 decision issued Friday, the court said even though Ottawa modified the law after the Supreme Court struck down much of it in 2023, the new version still infringes on provincial jurisdiction. The Court of Appeal found that, among other things, the act still gives Ottawa the power to stop a project in provincial jurisdiction if it has even the smallest impact on federal jurisdiction. "While Parliament may have the power to create an impact assessment scheme that complements existing regulation in environmental matters, the [Impact Assessment Act] creates great uncertainty due to the potential for previously unpronounced standards to apply to designated projects," the court wrote. Canada's top court rules environmental impact law unconstitutional "This merely exacerbates the concern that a federal assessment scheme might enable the federal government, on the pretext of some narrow ground of federal jurisdiction, to conduct a far-ranging inquiry into matters that are exclusively within provincial jurisdiction." The court said while some of the changes Ottawa made to the previous version of the act weren't constitutionally problematic, the law still gave Ottawa overly broad powers in areas of provincial jurisdiction. "The decision maker may regulate the project causing the impacts through imposition of conditions and followup programs, or indefinite prohibitions on entire projects and matters within provincial jurisdiction rather than confining oversight to federal effects caused by the project," the court wrote. Alberta challenge to federal project review law being heard in court, again Ontario and Saskatchewan both backed Alberta in its legal challenge. withheld.headline: City Council approves Toronto's 2026 budget with $63.1-billion capital plan, frozen TTC fares
withheld.evidence: The Canada Voice network · 13 local news sites across Ontario Toronto City Council has signed off on an $18.9-billion operating budget and the largest 10-year capital plan in the city's history, including frozen TTC fares and a property tax increase below inflation. October 10, 2026 at 6:18 p.m. · Updated October 11, 2026 at 2:10 p.m. · 2 min read Toronto City Council has approved the city's 2026 budget, signing off on an $18.9-billion operating plan and a 10-year capital budget that the city says is the largest in its history. The budget — Mayor Olivia Chow's third since her election in 2023 — was passed at a special meeting of council on Tuesday, according to a statement from Councillor Paula Fletcher , who represents Toronto-Danforth and published a budget breakdown on her website. The centrepiece of the plan is a $63.1-billion capital budget and plan covering 2026 to 2035, which Fletcher described as the biggest 10-year capital commitment the city has ever made. Fletcher said the budget's affordability measures — including frozen TTC fares and free meals for students — would save a working family with two children about $1,200 a year on groceries and transportation costs alone. The property tax increase for 2026 is set at 2.2 per cent, which Fletcher noted is below the rate of inflation. The budget also includes $788 million in new savings and efficiencies, according to Fletcher, who said the city's financial position has improved over the past two years under Chow's leadership. withheld.headline: China Unveils First Nationwide Labor Rules to Protect Gig Economy Workers
withheld.evidence: China’s labor ministry on Thursday released draft rules that would set nationwide protections for workers in the fast-growing gig economy, including minimum-pay safeguards, limits on algorithmic decision-making and stronger obligations for internet platforms. The Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security is seeking public comment through Nov. 8 on the 54-article draft, which would be China’s first ministerial regulation specifically governing the rights of workers in new forms of employment, such as food-delivery riders, couriers, ride-hailing drivers and truck drivers. withheld.headline: Syria Begins Destroying Chemical Weapons Remnants
withheld.evidence: Syria's Permanent Representative to the OPCW, Mohammad Katoub, announced that operations to destroy remnants of the Assad-era chemical program have begun, while warning that Israeli attacks hinder the process and that a timeframe for completion has not yet been set. Syria's Permanent Representative to the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), Mohammad Katoub, stated that his country continues full cooperation with the organisation's Technical Secretariat to completely eliminate remnants of the chemical weapons program from the Assad era. He confirmed that destruction operations have already begun, describing this as tangible progress in the capabilities of Syria's national teams working on this sensitive file. The announcement falls within an internationally monitored process overseen by the OPCW, the body responsible for verifying the elimination of banned weapons programs. Ongoing work includes verification, inspection, and destruction of remaining materials and facilities linked to the former program. Katoub pointed out that Israeli attacks constitute a real obstacle to the removal of the chemical program's remnants, imposing security challenges and operational complications on field teams. In practical terms, these obstacles tie the pace of work to security conditions at the affected sites, making movement, equipment handling, and field coordination more difficult.
